lessons.title: What Is Git?
lessons.lessonGoal: Understand what Git is, why version control exists, and how Git fundamentally differs from simply saving files or keeping manual backups.

sections.title: What Git Is
sections.content: Git is a distributed version control system: software that tracks every change made to a set of files over time, letting you save snapshots of your project's history, return to any previous snapshot, see exactly what changed and when, and work on multiple versions of a project simultaneously without losing anything. 'Distributed' means every developer's copy of a Git repository contains the full project history, not just the current files — there's no single central server required for Git itself to function, even though most teams choose to use one (like GitHub) for convenience and collaboration. Git was created in 2005 by Linus Torvalds (the creator of Linux) specifically to manage the famously large and fast-moving Linux kernel codebase, and has since become the dominant version control tool across virtually the entire software industry.

sections.title: A Video Game's Save System, Not A Single Save File
sections.content: Think of working without version control like playing a video game with only one save slot: if you make a mistake, you either live with it or start over from scratch, and you have no way to compare your current progress to where you were an hour ago. Git is like a video game with unlimited save slots, where every save records exactly what changed since the last one, with a note explaining why. You can jump back to any previous save instantly, compare two saves side by side to see exactly what's different, and even branch off into a completely separate save file to try something risky, all without ever losing your main progress. Folders named 'project_final', 'project_final_v2', and 'project_final_ACTUAL_FINAL' are the equivalent of a single save slot with manual, error-prone backups — Git replaces that entire fragile system with something precise and reliable.

sections.title: Git's Core Concepts At A Glance
sections.content:
- Repository (repo): a project folder that Git is tracking, containing the full history of every tracked change
- Commit: a saved snapshot of the project at a specific point in time, with a message describing what changed and why
- Working directory: the actual files on your computer as you're currently editing them
- Staging area: a holding zone where you choose exactly which changes will be included in your next commit, before actually committing them
- Repository history: the full sequence of commits, forming a timeline of every change ever made

These concepts will be explored in hands-on detail starting in the next lesson; this lesson focuses purely on understanding why this system exists and what problem it solves before diving into commands.

sections.title: How Git Tracks Changes Without Storing Full Copies Every Time
sections.content: A common misconception is that Git works like a series of full backup copies of your entire project, one per save. In reality, Git is much smarter: after an initial snapshot, it tracks changes efficiently by storing each commit as a snapshot of the entire project state, but uses compression and a content-addressable storage system (where identical file content is only stored once, referenced by a unique hash, even across multiple commits) to avoid wasting space on unchanged files. Every commit gets a unique identifier (a SHA-1 hash, a long string of letters and numbers) calculated from its content and history, meaning even a tiny one-character change produces an entirely new, unique commit identity — this is part of what makes Git's history tamper-evident and reliable as a record of exactly what happened and when.

sections.title: A Simple Mental Walkthrough Of Git's Workflow
sections.content: Before any real commands (covered next lesson), here's the conceptual loop Git revolves around, shown as plain steps rather than syntax:
sections.code:
1. You edit files in your working directory (write code as normal).
2. You decide which of those changes are ready to be saved
   as a meaningful unit -> you 'stage' them.
3. You commit the staged changes with a message describing
   what changed and why -> a new, permanent snapshot is created.
4. You repeat this loop many times throughout a project's life,
   building up a complete, readable history of how the project
   evolved, one deliberate snapshot at a time.

# This loop is the foundation everything else in this module builds on:
# branching, merging, and pull requests are all ways of managing
# multiple versions of this same commit history happening in parallel.
sections.explanation: Notice this workflow has a deliberate, two-step save process — staging, then committing — rather than Git automatically saving everything you type. This is intentional: it lets you choose exactly which changes belong together in a single, meaningful snapshot, rather than mixing unrelated changes into one unclear save point. The next lesson will translate this exact conceptual loop into real terminal commands.

sections.title: Where Git Is Used On Every Real Engineering Team
sections.content: Git is effectively universal in professional software development: every company you'll work for as a developer almost certainly uses Git, typically hosted on a platform like GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket. Beyond just personal backup, Git is the foundation that makes team collaboration possible at all — multiple developers can work on the same codebase simultaneously, in isolated branches, without overwriting each other's work, and merge their changes back together in a controlled, reviewable way (covered later in this module). Resumes and job applications in software development routinely expect Git fluency as baseline knowledge, not an advanced skill.

sections.title: What Goes Wrong Without Version Control
sections.content:
1. Manual folder-based 'versioning' (project_v1, project_v2, project_final) becomes unmanageable within days, with no clear record of exactly what changed between versions or why.

2. A single mistake or accidental deletion, without any saved history to recover from, can mean losing significant work entirely.

3. Multiple people editing the same files via shared drives or email attachments routinely overwrite each other's changes, since there's no mechanism for safely combining simultaneous edits.

4. Without a record of who changed what and when, diagnosing when and why a bug was introduced becomes a matter of guesswork rather than a quick, precise lookup.

5. Experimenting with a risky idea directly in your only copy of the project means any failed experiment can leave the project in a broken, hard-to-revert state.

sections.title: History As A Safety Net For Experimentation
sections.content: Git's deepest value isn't just backup — it's the psychological and practical safety net it provides for experimentation. Because every commit is a recoverable snapshot, and branches (covered later) let you try ideas in complete isolation from your main, working code, Git removes much of the fear around trying something that might not work. This directly enables better engineering: developers who know they can always get back to a known-good state are far more willing to refactor aggressively, try a riskier but potentially better approach, or make sweeping changes with confidence, compared to developers working without any safety net, who tend toward overly cautious, defensive coding habits purely out of fear of unrecoverable mistakes.

sections.title: Where To Verify Git Is Actually Installed And Working
sections.content: Before any of Git's features matter, confirming Git itself is correctly installed is the first troubleshooting step: running git --version in a terminal should print a version number; if instead you see a 'command not found' error, Git needs to be installed first (covered in the next lesson's setup). Once inside an actual Git repository, running git status is the single most useful command for understanding the current state — it shows which files have been changed, which changes are staged, and which are not yet tracked at all, and is the command experienced developers run constantly, almost as a reflex, before deciding what to do next.

checkpoints.question: What does it mean that Git is a 'distributed' version control system?
options: It only works when connected to the internet
Every developer's copy of the repository contains the full project history, not just the current files
It distributes files randomly across multiple computers
It requires a paid central server to function at all
checkpoints.explanation: Distributed means each local copy (clone) of a repository holds the complete history, not just a snapshot of current files, unlike older centralized version control systems.

checkpoints.question: What is a 'commit' in Git?
options: A folder containing the entire project
A saved snapshot of the project at a specific point in time, with a descriptive message
A backup stored only on GitHub's servers
The same thing as a branch
checkpoints.explanation: A commit is a recorded snapshot of the project's state at a given moment, accompanied by a message describing what changed.

checkpoints.question: A team has been manually managing versions using folders named project_v1, project_v2, and project_final. What is the most likely problem they'll eventually run into?
options: Nothing; this approach scales perfectly fine for any team size
No clear record of exactly what changed between versions, increased risk of overwritten work, and difficulty recovering from mistakes
Folders are faster than Git for large projects
This approach is actually how Git works internally
checkpoints.explanation: Manual folder-based versioning lacks precise change tracking, safe collaboration support, and reliable recovery — exactly the problems Git is designed to solve.

lessons.title: Version Control Basics
lessons.lessonGoal: Learn the core Git commands for initializing a repository, tracking changes, staging files, committing, and viewing history.

sections.title: From Concepts To Commands
sections.content: Lesson 1 introduced the concepts of repositories, staging, and commits; this lesson translates those concepts into the actual Git commands you'll type, almost daily, in a terminal. Git is primarily a command-line tool (though graphical interfaces exist), and learning its core commands directly — rather than only through a visual tool — is what gives you the flexibility to work in any environment, debug issues precisely, and understand exactly what's happening at each step rather than trusting a black-box button click.

sections.title: A Camera Taking Deliberate Photos, Not A Security Recording
sections.content: Think of git add as framing a photo — deciding exactly what should be in the shot — and git commit as actually pressing the shutter button to permanently capture that framed moment. Git doesn't work like a security camera, constantly and automatically recording everything; it requires you to deliberately choose what belongs in each 'photo' (commit) and when to take it. This is precisely why git add (staging) exists as a separate step from git commit: you might have made five different unrelated changes in your working directory, but only want two of them captured together in this particular photo, saving the other three for a separate, more focused photo later.

sections.title: Core Git Commands
sections.content:
- git init — initializes a new Git repository in the current folder, starting to track its history
- git status — shows the current state: which files are changed, staged, or untracked
- git add <filename> — stages a specific file's changes for the next commit
- git add . — stages all changed files in the current directory at once
- git commit -m "message" — commits the currently staged changes with a descriptive message
- git log — shows the commit history, most recent first, with commit hashes, authors, dates, and messages
- git diff — shows the exact line-by-line differences between your working directory and the last commit (or between staged and unstaged changes)
- .gitignore — a special file listing patterns for files/folders Git should never track (like node_modules/, .env files containing secrets, or OS-specific files like .DS_Store)

sections.title: What Actually Happens During git add And git commit
sections.content: When you run git add <file>, Git doesn't move or copy the file anywhere visible — it calculates a hash of the file's current content and records that hash in the staging area (technically called the 'index'), marking exactly this version of this file as ready for the next commit. If you then edit the file again before committing, those newer changes are NOT automatically included — you'd need to run git add again to update what's staged, which is a common point of confusion for beginners who expect committing to always capture whatever the file currently looks like. When you run git commit, Git takes everything currently staged, bundles it into a new commit object linked to the previous commit (forming the chain that makes up your project's history), and moves your branch pointer (more on branches in lesson 4) forward to point at this new commit.

sections.title: A Complete First Commit, Start To Finish
sections.content: This sequence shows the full basic workflow for starting to track a new project:
sections.code:
# Initialize a new repository in the current folder git init # Create a .gitignore so unwanted files are never tracked echo "node_modules/\n.env\n.DS_Store" > .gitignore # Check current status - everything will show as untracked git status # Stage all current files (respecting .gitignore automatically) git add . # Check status again - files now show as staged, ready to commit git status # Commit the staged snapshot with a clear, descriptive message git commit -m "Initial commit: project structure and basic HTML page" # View the commit history git log # Shows: commit hash, author, date, and the message above # Make a change to a file, then check the difference before staging echo "

New paragraph

" >> index.html git diff # Shows exactly which lines were added/changed since the last commit
sections.explanation: Each git status call shows a different stage of the same files' journey: untracked, then staged, then (after commit) clean again. The .gitignore file ensures things like node_modules/ (often containing thousands of files) are never accidentally tracked, which would otherwise bloat the repository enormously and isn't useful information to track anyway, since those files can always be regenerated. git diff before staging a new change lets you review exactly what you're about to add, a habit that prevents accidentally committing unintended changes (like leftover debugging console.log statements).

sections.title: How These Commands Are Used Daily On Real Teams
sections.content: git status and git diff are run constantly throughout a normal workday, almost as a reflex before staging or committing anything, to confirm exactly what's about to be saved. git log (often with additional flags like --oneline for a condensed view) is used to review recent history, find when a specific change was introduced, or locate a particular commit to reference or revert. A well-maintained .gitignore file is considered baseline professionalism on any real project — accidentally committing secrets (API keys, passwords) or massive dependency folders is a common, embarrassing, and sometimes serious mistake that a proper .gitignore prevents from the very first commit.

sections.title: Common Version Control Mistakes
sections.content:
1. Running git commit without first running git add, and being confused why 'nothing happened' — commit only captures what's currently staged, not automatically everything in the working directory.

2. Writing vague, unhelpful commit messages like "fix" or "updates", which provide no useful information when looking back through history later trying to find when and why a specific change was made (commit message quality is covered in depth in lesson 7).

3. Forgetting to create a .gitignore before the first commit, accidentally committing node_modules/ or sensitive .env files, which can be difficult to fully remove from history later even after deleting them in a subsequent commit.

4. Editing a file after staging it with git add, then committing, mistakenly believing the newer edits were included — only the staged version at the time of git add is captured unless git add is run again.

5. Treating git status and git diff as optional steps rather than habitual checks, leading to commits that accidentally include unrelated or unintended changes.

sections.title: Deliberate, Reviewable Units Of Change
sections.content: The two-step add-then-commit process exists to encourage a specific engineering discipline: each commit should represent one deliberate, coherent unit of change, ideally something you could describe in a single clear sentence. This matters enormously for anyone (including future you) trying to understand a project's history later — a history of small, well-described, focused commits is dramatically easier to navigate, review, and revert from than a history of occasional massive commits bundling dozens of unrelated changes together. Investing the small extra effort to stage and commit deliberately, rather than blindly running git add . and committing everything indiscriminately, pays off enormously the first time you need to find or undo a specific change months later.

sections.title: Using git status And git diff As Your First Diagnostic Steps
sections.content: Whenever you're unsure what state your repository is in — what's changed, what's staged, what's missing — git status should always be the very first command you run; it answers most basic 'what's going on' questions immediately and unambiguously. If something was committed that shouldn't have been, or a change doesn't look the way you expected, git diff (or git diff --staged to see exactly what's staged versus the last commit) shows the precise line-by-line difference, which is far more reliable than trying to remember what you changed from memory.

checkpoints.question: What does git add . do?
options: Permanently saves all changes with no way to undo them
Stages all changed files in the current directory, preparing them for the next commit
Deletes all untracked files
Creates a new branch
checkpoints.explanation: git add . stages all current changes in the working directory, marking them ready to be included in the next commit.

checkpoints.question: You run git add on a file, then make additional edits to that same file, then run git commit. What gets included in the commit?
options: Only the version of the file at the moment git add was run, not the later edits
Whatever the file currently looks like, including the later edits
Nothing, since the file was edited after staging
Git automatically merges both versions
checkpoints.explanation: Staging captures a snapshot of the file at that exact moment; edits made afterward are not included unless git add is run again before committing.

checkpoints.question: What is the purpose of a .gitignore file?
options: It lists commit messages that are not allowed
It specifies files and folders that Git should never track, like dependency folders or secret files
It deletes files from your computer automatically
It is required for git init to work at all
checkpoints.explanation: .gitignore prevents specified files and folders (like node_modules/ or .env) from ever being tracked or accidentally committed.

lessons.title: GitHub Introduction
lessons.lessonGoal: Understand the difference between Git and GitHub, and learn to push a local repository to a remote, clone existing repositories, and pull updates.

sections.title: Git Versus GitHub
sections.content: Git and GitHub are related but distinct: Git is the version control software itself, running entirely on your own computer, with no internet connection required for any of the commands from lesson 2. GitHub is a separate, internet-hosted platform and company that stores Git repositories remotely, adds a web interface for browsing code and history, and layers on collaboration features Git itself doesn't provide — pull requests, issue tracking, code review tools, and project management boards. You could use Git productively for your entire career without ever touching GitHub; GitHub simply makes hosting, sharing, and collaborating on Git repositories dramatically easier, which is why it (and similar platforms like GitLab and Bitbucket) has become essentially universal in professional software development.

sections.title: Your Personal Diary Versus A Shared Cloud Drive
sections.content: Think of a local Git repository like a personal diary you keep at home — entirely private, fully functional on its own, with a complete history only you can see. GitHub is like uploading that diary to a shared cloud drive: now others can view it (if you allow them), comment on specific entries, suggest their own additions, and you can access it from any computer, not just the one it was originally written on. The diary itself (your local Git history) doesn't fundamentally change by being uploaded — it's the same diary, just now also accessible and shareable from a central, always-available location that everyone with permission can reach.

sections.title: Core Remote Repository Commands
sections.content:
- git remote add origin <url> — connects your local repository to a remote one on GitHub, naming it 'origin' (a near-universal convention for your primary remote)
- git push origin main — uploads your local commits on the 'main' branch to the 'origin' remote
- git clone <url> — downloads an entire existing repository (with its full history) from a remote, creating a new local copy
- git pull — downloads and merges any new commits from the remote into your current local branch, keeping you in sync with changes others have pushed
- git push -u origin main — the -u flag sets 'origin main' as the default remote/branch for future plain 'git push' commands on this branch, so you don't need to specify them every time afterward

sections.title: How Local And Remote Histories Stay In Sync
sections.content: A remote repository (like one hosted on GitHub) is, structurally, just another copy of the same Git repository — it has its own commit history, which may be ahead of, behind, or diverged from your local copy at any given moment. git push uploads commits that exist locally but not yet on the remote, advancing the remote's history to match yours. git pull does the reverse: it downloads commits that exist on the remote but not yet locally, and merges them into your current branch. If both you and someone else have made different commits since the last sync, a pull may require Git to merge those two diverging histories together (covered in more depth in lesson 4 on branching/merging) — sometimes automatically, sometimes requiring you to manually resolve a conflict if the same lines were changed differently by both parties.

sections.title: Connecting A Local Repository To GitHub And Syncing
sections.content: This sequence shows taking the locally-initialized repository from lesson 2 and connecting it to a new, empty repository created on GitHub's website:
sections.code:
# After creating an empty repository on GitHub's website,
# connect your existing local repo to it as 'origin'
git remote add origin https://github.com/yourusername/your-repo.git

# Push your existing local commits up to GitHub for the first time,
# and set this as the default push target for this branch going forward
git push -u origin main

# Later, after making and committing more local changes:
git push
# (no need to specify origin/main again, thanks to -u above)

# If a teammate has pushed new commits since you last synced:
git pull
# downloads and merges their new commits into your local branch

# To start working on a completely different existing project from GitHub:
git clone https://github.com/someuser/some-project.git
# downloads the entire repository, including full history, into a new local folder
sections.explanation: git remote add origin only needs to be run once per repository, establishing the connection; after that, push and pull handle ongoing synchronization. Notice git clone is fundamentally different from git init — clone is for obtaining an existing project's complete history from somewhere else, while init starts a brand-new, empty history from scratch. Using git clone is almost always how you'll begin working on an existing team's codebase for the first time.

sections.title: GitHub As The Center Of Real Team Collaboration
sections.content: On virtually every professional engineering team, GitHub (or an equivalent platform) is the central hub: it's where code lives, where pull requests and code review happen (lesson 5), where issues and feature requests are tracked, and often where automated tests run on every change before it's allowed to merge. Open-source projects (lesson 8) are almost universally hosted on GitHub, making it the platform where millions of developers discover, use, and contribute to shared code. A GitHub profile, including its visible contribution history and public repositories, has also become a de facto portfolio that many employers look at directly when evaluating developer candidates.

sections.title: Common GitHub And Remote Mistakes
sections.content:
1. Trying to git push before ever running git remote add origin, resulting in an error because Git doesn't know where 'origin' should point yet.

2. Forgetting to git pull before starting new work when collaborating with others, leading to a diverged history that requires extra merging effort later that could have been avoided by syncing first.

3. Accidentally pushing committed secrets (API keys, passwords) to a public GitHub repository, which can expose sensitive credentials publicly and potentially require revoking and rotating those credentials entirely, not just deleting the file in a later commit (since the history would still contain it).

4. Confusing git clone (downloading a brand-new copy of an existing remote repo) with git pull (updating an already-existing local copy you're actively working in) — using clone repeatedly instead of pull can create confusing duplicate folders.

5. Not understanding repository visibility settings (public vs. private) on GitHub, and accidentally making sensitive or proprietary code publicly visible to anyone on the internet.

sections.title: Separating The Tool From The Platform
sections.content: Understanding that Git (the tool) and GitHub (one platform among several that hosts Git repositories) are separate things is a small but important example of a broader engineering habit: distinguishing a fundamental technology from any particular vendor or product built on top of it. This same separation appears constantly in engineering — SQL versus a specific database product, HTTP versus a specific web framework, containers versus a specific cloud provider's container service. Developers who understand the underlying fundamental (here, Git itself) can adapt quickly if a team or company uses a different platform (GitLab, Bitbucket, or a self-hosted Git server) built on the exact same underlying tool, rather than being stuck because they only ever learned one vendor's specific interface.

sections.title: Diagnosing Push, Pull, And Remote Connection Issues
sections.content: git remote -v lists all currently configured remotes and their URLs, which is the first thing to check if push or pull commands are failing with confusing errors — it confirms whether 'origin' is actually pointing where you expect. If a push is rejected with a message about the remote containing work you don't have locally, that's Git protecting you from accidentally overwriting someone else's commits; the fix is almost always to git pull first (resolving any conflicts if needed), then push again, rather than forcing the push through, which could destroy a teammate's work.

checkpoints.explanation: Git is the underlying version control tool, usable entirely locally; GitHub is one of several platforms that host Git repositories remotely and add features like pull requests and issue tracking.

lessons.title: Branching And Merging
lessons.lessonGoal: Understand what branches are, how to create and switch between them, how merging combines work from different branches, and how to resolve a basic merge conflict.

sections.title: What A Branch Is
sections.content: A branch is an independent line of development within a repository — essentially a separate, parallel copy of the project's history that you can change without affecting any other branch, including the main one. Every Git repository has at least one branch (conventionally named main), and creating a new branch lets you work on a new feature, fix a bug, or experiment with a risky idea in complete isolation, with the option to later merge those changes back into main once they're ready, or discard the branch entirely if the experiment didn't work out, leaving main completely untouched either way. Branching is what makes Git's 'safety net for experimentation' (from lesson 1) practically usable on real, ongoing projects, rather than just a theoretical benefit.

sections.title: A Tree With A Trunk And Separate Limbs
sections.content: Picture a tree, where the trunk represents your main branch — the stable, official version of the project. Creating a new branch is like growing a new limb that splits off from a specific point on the trunk: it can grow in its own direction, develop its own leaves (commits), without disturbing the trunk or any other limb at all. If that limb grows into something valuable, merging brings its growth back into the trunk, incorporating everything that limb developed. If the limb's growth turns out to be a dead end, you can simply prune it away (delete the branch) without the trunk ever having been affected. Multiple limbs can grow simultaneously from the same trunk, each developing independently — this is exactly how multiple developers (or you, working on multiple features) can make parallel progress without interfering with each other.

sections.title: Core Branching And Merging Commands
sections.content:
- git branch — lists all branches in the current repository, with an asterisk marking the one you're currently on
- git branch feature-login — creates a new branch named 'feature-login', without switching to it yet
- git checkout feature-login — switches your working directory to the specified branch (or git switch feature-login, a newer, clearer alternative command for the same purpose)
- git checkout -b feature-login — creates AND switches to a new branch in one step, the most common way to start new work
- git merge feature-login — run while on main, this combines feature-login's commits into main
- git branch -d feature-login — deletes a branch (typically after it's been merged and is no longer needed)

sections.title: How Git Merges Two Branches, And Why Conflicts Happen
sections.content: When you merge one branch into another, Git looks at the commit history of both branches since they diverged from a shared common ancestor commit, and attempts to automatically combine the changes. If the two branches changed completely different parts of the codebase (or even different lines within the same file), Git can almost always merge them automatically without any help. A merge conflict occurs specifically when both branches changed the exact same lines of the exact same file in different, incompatible ways — Git has no way to know which version you actually want, so it pauses the merge and asks you to manually decide. Git marks the conflicting section directly inside the affected file using special markers (<<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>>) showing both versions side by side, and resolving the conflict means editing that section to keep the correct final content, removing the markers, then staging and committing the resolved file to complete the merge.

sections.title: Creating A Branch, Making Changes, Merging, And Resolving A Conflict
sections.content: This sequence shows a typical branching workflow, including what a conflict resolution looks like:
sections.code:
# Create and switch to a new branch for a specific feature
git checkout -b feature-dark-mode

# Make changes, then stage and commit them on this branch
echo ".dark-mode { background: #111; color: #eee; }" >> styles.css
git add styles.css
git commit -m "Add dark mode styles"

# Switch back to main to merge the finished feature in
git checkout main
git merge feature-dark-mode
# If no conflicting changes exist, this merges automatically

# Clean up the now-merged branch
git branch -d feature-dark-mode

# --- If a conflict had occurred instead, styles.css might show: ---
# <<<<<<< HEAD
# body { background: white; color: black; }
# =======
# .dark-mode { background: #111; color: #eee; }
# >>>>>>> feature-dark-mode
#
# You would manually edit this section to the correct final version,
# remove all three marker lines, then:
git add styles.css
git commit -m "Resolve merge conflict: combine light and dark mode styles"
sections.explanation: The feature branch isolates the dark mode work entirely until it's ready, at which point merging on main brings it in as a clean, deliberate step. The commented conflict example shows exactly what Git inserts directly into a file when automatic merging isn't possible — the section between <<<<<<< HEAD and ======= is what main currently has, and the section between ======= and >>>>>>> feature-dark-mode is what the incoming branch has; resolving means manually deciding what the final combined code should actually be.

sections.title: How Branching Structures Real Team Workflows
sections.content: Virtually every professional team uses a 'feature branch' workflow: main (or sometimes a similarly protected branch) always represents stable, working code, and all new work happens on separate branches, merged back in only after review (pull requests, covered next lesson). This lets dozens of developers work simultaneously on completely different features without ever blocking each other, and lets a team selectively merge only the features that are actually ready, while others continue development uninterrupted. Branch naming conventions (like feature/, bugfix/, or including a ticket number) are common team practices that make a repository's branch list immediately scannable and meaningful.

sections.title: Common Branching And Merging Mistakes
sections.content:
1. Making significant changes directly on main instead of a feature branch, losing the isolation and safety that branching is specifically designed to provide.

2. Panicking when a merge conflict appears, rather than recognizing it as a normal, expected part of collaborative development that simply requires a manual decision about which (or what combination) of two changes should win.

3. Resolving a conflict by carelessly keeping one version entirely without actually reading both sides, potentially discarding meaningful work from the other branch.

4. Forgetting to delete merged branches, leading to a cluttered, confusing branch list over time that makes it hard to tell what's still active work versus already-completed, merged history.

5. Letting a feature branch diverge from main for a very long time without merging or syncing, which dramatically increases both the number and complexity of conflicts that eventually need to be resolved all at once.

sections.title: Isolating Risk Through Parallel, Independent Work
sections.content: Branching embodies a recurring engineering principle: isolate risky or in-progress work from stable, working systems, so that a mistake or incomplete idea in one place cannot destabilize everything else. This same principle reappears constantly beyond Git — staging environments separate from production servers, feature flags that let new code exist without being active for all users, and modular code architecture that prevents a bug in one module from automatically breaking unrelated ones. Recognizing branching as one specific implementation of this broader 'isolate before integrating' pattern helps the concept transfer naturally to other engineering contexts later in your career.

sections.title: Diagnosing Which Branch You're On And What's Different
sections.content: git branch (with no arguments) immediately shows every branch and marks your current one with an asterisk — the first thing to check if you're ever unsure where you are, especially before making changes you intend to keep isolated. git status, while on any branch, also shows the current branch name at the top of its output. When resolving a conflict, carefully reading both sides of the <<<<<<< / ======= / >>>>>>> markers, and testing the resulting code after resolution (not just assuming the conflict markers were removed correctly), is essential — a conflict resolved incorrectly can silently reintroduce a bug that the original conflict was actually flagging.

checkpoints.question: What does git checkout -b feature-login do?
options: Deletes the feature-login branch
Creates a new branch named feature-login and immediately switches to it
Merges feature-login into main
Only switches to an existing feature-login branch without creating anything
checkpoints.explanation: The -b flag combined with checkout both creates a new branch and switches to it in a single command.

checkpoints.question: You run git merge feature-x while on main, and Git reports a merge conflict in styles.css. What does this mean?
options: Git has permanently corrupted the file
Both main and feature-x changed the exact same lines of styles.css in different, incompatible ways, requiring a manual decision
The merge failed completely and no changes were applied at all
feature-x must be deleted before merging can succeed
checkpoints.explanation: A merge conflict happens specifically when both branches modified the same lines differently; Git pauses and asks for manual resolution since it can't automatically decide which version is correct.

checkpoints.question: Why do teams typically avoid making significant changes directly on the main branch?
options: main cannot accept any commits at all
Working directly on main loses the isolation that feature branches provide, risking instability in the project's primary, working version
It is technically impossible to commit to main
main automatically deletes itself if changed directly
checkpoints.explanation: Feature branches isolate in-progress or risky work, keeping main stable; working directly on main removes that safety net.

lessons.title: Pull Requests
lessons.lessonGoal: Understand what a pull request is, why it exists as a review gate before merging, and how to write one that's clear and easy for a reviewer to evaluate.

sections.title: What A Pull Request Is
sections.content: A pull request (PR) — sometimes called a merge request on platforms like GitLab — is a formal request, made on a platform like GitHub, to merge the changes from one branch into another (usually into main), accompanied by a description of what changed and why, a visible diff of every line changed, and a space for reviewers to leave comments, request changes, or approve the work before it's actually merged. Pull requests are not a Git feature at all — they're a GitHub (and similar platforms') feature built on top of Git's branching and merging, specifically to add a structured review step into the merge process rather than allowing direct, unreviewed merges into important branches.

sections.title: Submitting A Manuscript To An Editor, Not Publishing Directly
sections.content: Think of pushing directly to main without review like a writer self-publishing a manuscript the moment they finish typing the last word — no second pair of eyes ever sees it before it reaches the public. A pull request is like submitting that manuscript to an editor first: the editor reads through it, leaves comments on unclear passages, asks questions about ambiguous decisions, perhaps suggests changes, and only once it's been reviewed and refined does it actually get published. The manuscript isn't worse for having gone through review — it's almost always better, having benefited from a second perspective catching issues the original writer was too close to the work to notice themselves. This is exactly the role a pull request plays for code: a deliberate pause for review before changes become part of the permanent, shared codebase.

sections.title: The Typical Pull Request Lifecycle
sections.content:
1. Push a feature branch to GitHub: git push -u origin feature-branch-name
2. On GitHub's website, open a new pull request, choosing the feature branch as the source and main as the target
3. Write a clear title and description: what changed, why, and any context a reviewer needs (screenshots for visual changes, links to related issues, testing notes)
4. Reviewers examine the diff, leave comments, and either approve or request changes
5. If changes are requested, you push additional commits to the same branch, which automatically update the open pull request
6. Once approved, the pull request is merged (often via a button directly on GitHub, which runs the equivalent of git merge on the platform's servers)
7. The feature branch is typically deleted after a successful merge, the same cleanup step from lesson 4, but now often available as a one-click option on the platform itself

sections.title: What's Actually Happening Behind The Pull Request Interface
sections.content: Underneath GitHub's pull request interface, the underlying mechanics are exactly the branching and merging concepts from lesson 4 — a pull request is essentially a managed, reviewable wrapper around a git merge that hasn't happened yet. The diff shown in a pull request is computed the same way git diff works locally, comparing the feature branch against the target branch. Many teams configure 'branch protection rules' on important branches like main, which technically prevent direct pushes or merges without going through a pull request and meeting specific requirements first (a minimum number of approvals, passing automated tests, no unresolved comments) — enforcing the review process as a hard requirement rather than relying purely on team discipline or convention.

sections.title: From Feature Branch To A Well-Written Pull Request
sections.content: This example shows the Git commands leading up to a pull request, followed by an example of well-written PR description text (which would be typed into GitHub's web interface, not a terminal command):
sections.code:
# After committing your work on a feature branch locally (from lesson 4):
git push -u origin feature-dark-mode

# Now on GitHub's website, you'd open a pull request from
# feature-dark-mode into main, with a description like:

"""
Title: Add dark mode toggle to settings page

What changed:
- Added a dark mode CSS class and toggle button in settings.html
- Persisted the user's preference using localStorage so it
  survives a page reload
- Updated existing components to respect the dark mode class

Why:
Users have requested a dark mode option (see issue #42).
This implements the first version covering the settings
and dashboard pages; other pages will follow in a separate PR.

How to test:
1. Open the settings page
2. Click the dark mode toggle
3. Refresh the page and confirm dark mode persists

Screenshots:
[before/after screenshots would go here]
"""
sections.explanation: Notice the description answers exactly the questions a reviewer needs answered without having to ask: what changed, why it matters, how to verify it actually works, and visual confirmation via screenshots. This level of detail respects the reviewer's time and dramatically speeds up the review process, compared to a bare pull request with no description at all, which forces the reviewer to reverse-engineer context from the diff alone.

sections.title: Pull Requests As The Core Collaboration Loop On Real Teams
sections.content: On almost every professional engineering team, the pull request is the central unit of collaborative work — not the individual commit, and not the individual line of code, but the reviewable, mergeable bundle of changes that constitute one complete piece of work. Code review through pull requests serves multiple purposes simultaneously: catching bugs before they reach production, spreading knowledge of the codebase across the team (since reviewers see code they didn't write themselves), maintaining consistent code style and patterns, and creating a natural mentorship opportunity where more experienced developers can give feedback to less experienced ones directly in context. Many teams also run automated tests and linters automatically on every pull request, blocking merges if anything fails, adding a layer of automated review alongside human review.

sections.title: Common Pull Request Mistakes
sections.content:
1. Opening a pull request with a vague title like "updates" and no description at all, forcing reviewers to read through the entire diff with zero context about intent or scope.

2. Bundling many unrelated changes into one enormous pull request, making it exhausting and error-prone for a reviewer to evaluate thoroughly, and increasing the chance that an unrelated, low-priority change accidentally blocks an urgent one from being approved.

3. Taking review feedback personally or defensively, rather than treating it as the entire point of the process — catching issues before they reach production, the same way an editor's feedback is meant to improve a manuscript, not criticize the writer.

4. Merging your own pull request without waiting for review on a team that has agreed review is required, undermining the entire purpose of having a review step.

5. Letting a pull request sit open and un-reviewed for a long time, during which the underlying main branch continues to change, increasing the eventual merge conflict risk the longer the PR remains unmerged.

sections.title: Review As A Feature, Not An Obstacle
sections.content: It's tempting, especially early in a career, to view code review as a bureaucratic hurdle slowing down 'real' work. Experienced engineers instead recognize review as a core part of how high-quality software actually gets built: a second perspective consistently catches issues the original author, too close to their own code, would otherwise miss — edge cases, unclear naming, a simpler approach that wasn't considered, an assumption that doesn't hold in some other part of the codebase. Writing pull requests that make review easy (clear descriptions, focused scope, helpful context) is itself a skill that distinguishes more experienced developers, since it demonstrates an understanding that the goal isn't just 'getting code merged' but getting good code merged with the team's shared understanding intact.

sections.title: When A Pull Request Shows Unexpected Conflicts Or Changes
sections.content: If a pull request's diff shows far more changes than expected, the most common cause is that the feature branch was created from an outdated point in main's history, or unrelated commits accidentally ended up on the same branch — checking git log on the feature branch (and comparing it against main's log) usually reveals exactly which commits are actually unique to this branch versus inherited unexpectedly. If GitHub reports the PR has conflicts that must be resolved before merging, this is the exact same kind of merge conflict from lesson 4, just surfaced through the platform's interface rather than your local terminal — resolving it typically means pulling the latest main locally, merging it into your feature branch, resolving any conflicts there, and pushing the resolved branch back up.

checkpoints.question: What is a pull request, fundamentally?
options: A core feature of Git itself, available in every Git installation
A platform feature (like on GitHub) that adds a structured review step before merging one branch's changes into another
A command that automatically fixes merge conflicts
A way to permanently delete a branch's history
checkpoints.explanation: Pull requests are a platform-level feature built on top of Git's branching and merging, adding review, discussion, and approval before changes are merged.

checkpoints.question: A teammate opens a pull request titled 'updates' with no description, containing changes to five unrelated files. What is the most likely consequence?
options: Nothing; reviewers always have full context regardless of description quality
Reviewers will struggle to understand the intent and scope, slowing down review and increasing the chance of missed issues
GitHub will automatically reject pull requests without descriptions
The pull request will merge itself automatically
checkpoints.explanation: A vague title and missing description force reviewers to reverse-engineer context from the diff alone, making review slower and less effective.

checkpoints.question: What is one key purpose of code review through pull requests, beyond catching bugs?
options: Slowing down development for its own sake
Spreading knowledge of the codebase across the team and maintaining consistent patterns
Replacing the need for any testing entirely
Eliminating the need for clear commit messages
checkpoints.explanation: Code review also spreads codebase knowledge across the team, maintains consistency, and creates mentorship opportunities, in addition to catching bugs.

lessons.title: Collaboration Workflow
lessons.lessonGoal: Understand how branching, pull requests, issues, and team conventions combine into a complete, repeatable collaboration workflow used on real software teams.

sections.title: What A Collaboration Workflow Is
sections.content: A collaboration workflow is the agreed-upon set of practices a team follows for how work moves from an idea to a deployed feature — combining everything from this module so far (branches, commits, pull requests) with additional structure: how work is tracked and assigned (issues), what naming conventions are used, when and how often code is merged, and what quality gates (review, automated tests) must pass before code reaches main. Individual Git commands are the same regardless of team; what differs between teams is the workflow — the conventions and process layered on top of those commands that make many people's work fit together predictably and smoothly.

sections.title: Traffic Laws, Not Just Steering Wheels
sections.content: Knowing how to operate a car (steering, braking, accelerating — the equivalent of knowing individual Git commands) doesn't by itself let many drivers safely share the same roads. Traffic laws — which side to drive on, who has right of way, what a red light means — are what make it possible for many independent drivers to coexist on shared roads without constant collisions. A team's collaboration workflow plays exactly this role for code: it's the agreed-upon 'traffic laws' (always branch from main, always open a pull request, never force-push to main, link every branch to an issue) that let many developers, each capable of using Git's commands individually, work on the same shared codebase without constantly colliding with each other's work.

sections.title: Components Of A Typical Team Workflow
sections.content:
- Issues: a tracked unit of work (a bug report, feature request, or task) on GitHub, often with a number (e.g. #42) that can be referenced in commit messages and pull requests to link related work together
- Branch naming conventions: a consistent pattern like feature/42-dark-mode or bugfix/58-search-crash, making the purpose of any branch immediately clear from its name alone
- Definition of done: a team's shared understanding of what 'finished' actually means for a piece of work — commonly including passing tests, completed code review, and updated documentation, not just 'the code runs on my machine'
- Review requirements: how many approvals are needed, and whether specific people (e.g. the original code's owner) must review certain changes
- Merge strategy: whether merged pull requests are combined as a single 'squash commit' (cleaner history, common on many teams) or preserve every individual commit from the feature branch
- Continuous Integration (CI): automated systems that run tests and checks on every pull request automatically, covered in more depth in later modules, but relevant here as a workflow gate that often must pass before merging is allowed

sections.title: How These Pieces Connect Into One Coherent Loop
sections.content: These components aren't independent — they form a connected loop. An issue is created describing needed work, a branch is created referencing that issue's number, commits on that branch reference the issue in their messages where relevant, a pull request is opened that also references and will automatically close the issue upon merging (GitHub supports special keywords like 'Closes #42' in a PR description for this), automated CI checks run against the PR, human reviewers evaluate the actual logic and approach, and only once both automated and human review pass does the merge happen, which (depending on the team's GitHub configuration) can automatically close the original issue. This entire loop creates full traceability: months later, anyone can look at a specific line of code, trace it to the commit that introduced it, the pull request that merged it, and the original issue that motivated it in the first place.

sections.title: A Complete Workflow Loop, Issue To Merge
sections.content: This walks through one full cycle of the connected workflow described above:
sections.code:
# 1. An issue is created on GitHub: "#67: Add loading spinner during data fetch"

# 2. A branch is created referencing that issue number
git checkout -b feature/67-loading-spinner

# 3. Work happens, with commit messages referencing the issue where helpful
git add .
git commit -m "Add loading spinner component (refs #67)"

# 4. The branch is pushed and a pull request is opened on GitHub, with a
#    description that includes the special closing keyword:
#    "Closes #67"
git push -u origin feature/67-loading-spinner

# 5. Automated CI runs tests automatically against the PR (handled by
#    the platform, not a manual command)

# 6. A teammate reviews the PR, leaves a comment requesting a small
#    change, you push an additional commit addressing it:
git add .
git commit -m "Address review feedback: adjust spinner timing"
git push

# 7. Once approved and CI passes, the PR is merged on GitHub (often
#    via a button), which automatically closes issue #67 because of
#    the "Closes #67" keyword used in step 4

# 8. The feature branch is deleted, completing the loop
git checkout main
git pull
git branch -d feature/67-loading-spinner
sections.explanation: Every step in this loop references the same originating issue (#67), creating an unbroken chain of traceability from initial request through to final merged code. None of the individual Git commands here are new — they're exactly the commands from lessons 2 through 5 — but the consistent referencing convention (the issue number appearing in the branch name, commit messages, and PR description) is what elevates individual commands into an actual team workflow.

sections.title: Where This Full Workflow Shows Up On Real Teams
sections.content: Nearly every well-run engineering team follows some version of this issue-to-merge loop, even if specific conventions vary (some teams use Jira or Linear instead of GitHub Issues for tracking, for example, but link to those tickets the same way). New developers joining a team are typically expected to learn that team's specific workflow conventions within their first days, since the underlying Git commands themselves are assumed knowledge by the time someone is hired. Engineering managers and tech leads often care deeply about workflow discipline (clear issue descriptions, focused PRs, fast review turnaround) because it directly affects how quickly and reliably a team can ship software, independent of any individual developer's raw coding speed.

sections.title: Common Collaboration Workflow Breakdowns
sections.content:
1. Skipping issue tracking entirely, leading to work that's hard to prioritize, easy to forget, and impossible to trace back to its original motivation later.

2. Inconsistent or absent branch naming conventions, making a repository's branch list an unreadable mess where no one can tell what's active, abandoned, or already merged.

3. A team agreeing on a workflow in theory but not actually following it consistently in practice, which tends to erode trust and predictability over time as some pull requests skip review while others don't.

4. Confusion about merge strategy (squash vs. preserving individual commits) leading to a history that's either too compressed to understand individual changes, or too noisy with many small 'fix typo' commits cluttering meaningful history.

5. Treating CI failures as optional or 'probably fine to ignore', undermining the entire purpose of automated checks meant to catch issues before merge.

sections.title: Process As A Force Multiplier, Not Bureaucracy
sections.content: A thoughtfully designed collaboration workflow is what allows a team's overall output to be genuinely greater than the sum of its individual developers' raw coding speed — by reducing miscommunication, catching issues earlier (through review and CI) rather than later (in production), and creating a traceable history that saves enormous time during debugging or onboarding new team members. The instinct to dismiss process as 'bureaucracy slowing me down' usually reflects a narrow view focused only on an individual's immediate task; experienced engineers recognize that workflow conventions exist precisely because uncoordinated individual speed, without any shared structure, tends to produce slower, less reliable team-level outcomes overall, even if any single person's commits looked fast in isolation.

sections.title: Diagnosing A Broken Or Confusing Workflow
sections.content: When a team's workflow feels chaotic — unclear what's actually being worked on, pull requests sitting unreviewed for weeks, frequent merge conflicts — the root cause is rarely a Git command being used incorrectly; it's almost always a missing or inconsistently followed convention. Reviewing a repository's recent issues, branch names, and pull request descriptions for consistency (or the lack of it) is usually the fastest way to diagnose exactly where a team's workflow has broken down, the same way you'd review git status and git diff to diagnose a confusing individual repository state in earlier lessons, just applied at the team-process level instead of the single-repository level.

checkpoints.question: What is the main difference between knowing individual Git commands and following a team's collaboration workflow?
options: There is no difference; they are the same thing
A workflow layers shared conventions (issue tracking, naming, review requirements) on top of the same underlying Git commands to coordinate many people's work
Workflows replace the need to use Git commands at all
Workflows only matter for teams larger than 100 people
checkpoints.explanation: The underlying Git commands stay the same; a workflow adds the shared conventions and process that let many people's individual command usage fit together coherently.

checkpoints.question: A pull request description includes the text 'Closes #67'. What does this typically do on GitHub once the PR is merged?
options: Nothing; it's just a comment with no functional effect
It automatically closes issue #67, linking the merged work directly back to its original tracked request
It deletes issue #67 permanently
It prevents the PR from being merged until issue #67 is manually closed first
checkpoints.explanation: GitHub recognizes closing keywords like 'Closes #67' and automatically closes the referenced issue once the pull request is merged, maintaining traceability.

checkpoints.question: Why might a team's overall delivery speed suffer even if individual developers are each fast at writing code, in the absence of a clear collaboration workflow?
options: Individual speed always guarantees fast team output regardless of process
Without shared conventions, miscommunication, inconsistent review, and untraceable work tend to slow the team down overall, despite individual speed
Workflows are purely about looking organized and have no real effect on outcomes
Fast individual coding always compensates for any lack of process
checkpoints.explanation: A good workflow coordinates many people's work, reducing miscommunication and rework; without it, uncoordinated individual speed often doesn't translate into fast team-level delivery.

codingChallenge.title: Write Out A Complete Issue-To-Merge Workflow
codingChallenge.description: Pick a small hypothetical feature (e.g. 'add a contact form'). Write the complete sequence of actions from issue creation through final merge, referencing a consistent issue number throughout (in the branch name, at least one commit message, and the pull request description's closing keyword).

# TODO: create a branch referencing that issue number
# TODO: commit work with a message referencing the issue
# TODO: push and describe opening a PR with a closing keyword

# TODO: describe the merge and branch cleanup
